questions.topic: ICH Q10 goal of technology transfer
questions.question: This guide cites ICH Q10. What is the goal of technology transfer activities?

options.A: To transfer approved marketing authorization data from one regulatory authority to another so that a company can complete filings in several regions at the same time
options.B: To transfer product and process knowledge between development and manufacturing, and within or between manufacturing sites, to achieve product realisation
options.C: To transfer ownership and maintenance responsibility of equipment from the equipment supplier to the user, and to establish a maintenance program, spare parts inventory, and supplier audits after equipment acceptance
options.D: To transfer release authority from the quality unit to the production unit to shorten the time needed for batch release

questions.explanation: ICH Q10 section 3.1.2 defines technology transfer as the transfer of product and process knowledge, which is the basis for the manufacturing process, control strategy, process validation approach, and continual improvement. It is not a transfer of documents between regulators, and it does not involve transfer of equipment ownership or release authority.

questions.question: A company is going to contract a CMO to manufacture its product, and QA asks how to handle the quality agreement. According to this guide, which of the following is correct?

options.A: It can be handled as an appendix to the commercial supply agreement, covering only price, delivery time, and release specifications
options.B: It is needed only when the CMO is located overseas, focuses on batch release and document retention periods, and is kept by each party's QA separately
options.C: The receiving unit can set it unilaterally, without covering data integrity and information systems, and without review and sign-off by the sending unit
options.D: It is required when a contract partner is used, should be a separate document, and should cover data integrity, data management and responsibilities, IT requirements, and CPV reporting

questions.explanation: The guide states that a quality agreement is needed when a contract partner is used, that it should be a separate document, and that it should cover data integrity, data management and responsibilities, IT requirements, CPV and its reporting, continual improvement, and so on. Folding it into a commercial contract or narrowing its content does not match the text.

questions.topic: Scope and completion of a transfer
questions.question: At what point does this guide consider a technology transfer complete, so that CPV and CQV are outside its scope?

options.A: After the close-out phase; CPV and CQV are activities that take place after the transfer is complete
options.B: After release of the first PPQ batch; CPV is regarded as the last formal step of the transfer
options.C: At the end of the operational readiness phase; subsequent qualification is outside the transfer scope
options.D: After marketing authorization approval is obtained; CPV is regarded as the final determination of whether the transfer succeeded

questions.explanation: Section 1.3 explains that the guide treats the point after the close-out phase as the completion of a transfer, so CPV and CQV are out of scope. However, process validation is an important step in confirming that the transfer is complete, and the guide still briefly describes the relationship in Table 1.1.

questions.question: A project team needs to write a document that builds on the technology transfer proposal, describes the technical and project management elements in more detail, includes risk assessment and mitigation, is used to track progress, and is managed under formal change control. Which document is this?

options.A: Technology transfer charter, used to capture strategic intent and define the overall scope and team roles
options.B: Technology transfer protocol, used to define specific transfer activities, acceptance criteria, and success criteria
options.C: Technology transfer plan, used to align the team on specific activities, track project progress, and incorporate mitigation actions
options.D: Technology transfer package, used to compile all the knowledge needed to execute the process and analyze the product

questions.explanation: Key Terms explains that the plan is based on the proposal, incorporates the gap analysis, risk assessment, and mitigation actions, and should be managed under formal change control. The charter, protocol, and package each have their own definitions, but none is the detailed execution document built on the proposal.

questions.question: According to Table 1.1, in the correspondence between technology transfer and process validation, what role does PPQ play in the transfer?

options.A: Confirming that the receiving unit's utilities and equipment can operate within the ranges required for the CPPs
options.B: Confirming that the receiving unit is able to deliver the CQAs
options.C: Ensuring that the receiving unit has a monitoring mechanism in place to demonstrate that the transfer has been successfully delivered
options.D: Clarifying what needs to be transferred, such as CQAs, CPPs, material attributes, and the control strategy

questions.explanation: In Table 1.1, PPQ corresponds to "confirming the receiving unit can deliver the CQAs." Confirming that utilities and equipment operate within the ranges required for the CPPs is utilities and equipment qualification; ensuring a monitoring mechanism that shows the transfer was successfully delivered is CPV; and clarifying what needs to be transferred is the understanding needed in the Process Design stage.

questions.question: A project uses a RACI matrix to clarify roles. Which type of role does the "A" represent?

options.A: The person with ultimate accountability and authority, to whom the person in the "R" role is answerable
options.B: The person ultimately responsible for successfully delivering the project or task, that is, the one who actually gets the work done
options.C: The person whose opinion adds value and whose buy-in is needed for implementation
options.D: The person or group who needs to be informed of results or actions but does not take part in the decision process

questions.explanation: In RACI, the A stands for Accountable: the person with ultimate accountability and authority, to whom the R is answerable. The person ultimately responsible for successful delivery who actually does the work is the R (Responsible), the person whose opinion adds value is Consulted, and the person or group who needs to be informed of results is Informed.

questions.question: What does this guide say about who owns the risk assessments in a technology transfer?

options.A: The project manager usually owns the technical risk assessment, and the technical team owns the project risk assessment
options.B: The project manager usually owns the project risk assessment, and the technical team owns the technical risk assessment
options.C: The quality assurance department owns all risk assessments, and the project manager and technical team only provide input
options.D: Risk assessments are always owned by the sending unit, and the receiving unit is only responsible for carrying out mitigation actions

questions.explanation: Section 2.2.6 notes that risk assessments can be divided into types such as project, process, product, and equipment, and that owners and focus can differ; usually the project manager owns the project risk assessment and the technical team owns the technical risk assessment. QRM is also an iterative activity and is not owned by only one party.

questions.question: According to Chapter 2, which of the following best matches the basic definition of a "successful technology transfer"?

options.A: The receiving unit completes one engineering batch with test results within specification, after which no further assessment is needed
options.B: The sending unit completes delivery of documents and the receiving unit has signed for the technology transfer package
options.C: The receiving unit can routinely reproduce the transferred product, process, or method against predefined specifications agreed with the sending unit
options.D: The receiving unit's process yield is higher than the highest record the sending unit has ever achieved

questions.explanation: Section 2.3 states that the transfer is regarded as successful when the receiving unit can routinely reproduce the transferred product, process, or method against predefined specifications agreed with the sending unit and/or the development unit. Success criteria should be established in advance and assessed throughout the project, not judged from a single batch result or document sign-off.

questions.question: When writing a technology transfer charter, which of the following is consistent with this guide regarding "scope"?

options.A: Only the included items need to be listed; items outside the scope need not be recorded, to avoid limiting project flexibility
options.B: The scope is defined unilaterally by the receiving unit, and the sending unit only confirms it, without taking part
options.C: Once approved, the scope is fixed, and the project need not be reassessed even if charter elements change
options.D: The scope includes the project overview and business drivers; items out of scope are equally important and must be recorded

questions.explanation: Section 3.1.2 states that the scope in the charter includes the project overview and business drivers, and that items out of scope are equally important. Key Terms also notes that if charter elements change, the project must be reassessed regardless of the stage it has reached, and that the charter must be approved by stakeholders on both sides.

questions.topic: Control strategy ownership in the package
questions.question: At a transfer meeting, someone proposes that the technology transfer team determine the relationship between quality attributes and process parameters to serve as the basis of the control strategy. How should this be answered according to the guide?

options.A: This is not the role of technology transfer; the control strategy is usually established during process development, and the transfer must make it available to the receiving unit and ensure it can be executed
options.B: This is the core task of the technology transfer team, and the receiving unit should re-establish the relationships of all quality attributes and parameters during the transfer
options.C: This applies only to legacy products; for new products the receiving unit's quality department sets the control strategy itself and is responsible for approving it
options.D: This can be done only after PPQ is complete, and during the transfer only the process flow diagram and historical data need to be delivered

questions.explanation: The Note in section 3.2.2 states explicitly that identifying quality attributes, process parameters, and their relationships is not the role of technology transfer; it is the basis of the control strategy usually defined during process development. The transfer package must give the receiving unit the control strategy and its scientific rationale and ensure that it can be executed.

questions.question: A team assesses a gap with a risk estimation matrix and the overall risk is high. According to section 3.3.2, how should it be handled?

options.A: Simply document the rationale for acceptance and proceed, the same as for medium risk, and explain it in the close-out report
options.B: Proceed to PPQ and observe the actual results; if nothing abnormal occurs, no separate risk mitigation is needed
options.C: After communicating with management it can be accepted directly, with mitigation actions added only at the close-out stage
options.D: The risk is unacceptable and mitigation action must be taken, such as modifying or purchasing facilities or equipment, laboratory studies, or collecting more information

questions.explanation: High risk is regarded as unacceptable and must be mitigated to an acceptable level; actions can include facility or equipment modifications, laboratory studies, or additional information. Only medium risk might be accepted with a documented rationale; low risk is generally acceptable and needs no mitigation.

questions.question: An unexplained process shift occurs during the first large-scale runs. The receiving unit had established a small-scale model beforehand in the operational readiness phase. What use does the guide recommend?

options.A: Stop using it before GMP batches begin and replace it with document review, to keep small-scale results from interfering with large-scale batch decisions
options.B: Use it only for staff training, and archive it once operations start, without running it in parallel with large-scale batches
options.C: Run it in satellite mode in parallel with the early large-scale batches, using the same buffers or media, to provide a comparison for some parameters and help troubleshoot
options.D: Run it only after the large-scale batch ends, to confirm the final release result and as part of the batch record

questions.explanation: Section 3.4 recommends running the small-scale model in satellite mode in parallel during the early large-scale runs, using the same buffers or media, so that it helps troubleshoot large-scale problems by providing a comparison. It can also be used for process training, and its performance should be shown to be as expected before the large-scale runs.

questions.question: What does section 3.4 require regarding the order of analytical method qualification and full-scale process qualification?

options.A: The method can be qualified after PPQ is finished, with no need to document any particular risk
options.B: The method should be qualified first; if it runs in parallel with process qualification, the risk must be documented and accepted by management
options.C: Only compendial methods need to be qualified first; other methods can proceed together with the process
options.D: Method qualification is the responsibility of the sending unit, and the receiving unit simply adopts the results at PPQ

questions.explanation: Analytical methods must be qualified before full-scale process qualification so that process performance can be measured. If the two run in parallel, the risk to the overall qualification must be documented and accepted by management.

questions.question: The receiving unit's process (or analytical method) qualification fails to meet the acceptance criteria. According to section 3.5, what is the next step?

options.A: Investigate and address the cause of the failure before repeating the qualification
options.B: Simply repeat the same qualification; consecutive successes allow the earlier failure to be ignored
options.C: Relax the acceptance criteria to fit the existing data, and explain the difference in the report
options.D: Terminate the transfer project and have the sending unit arrange another receiving unit to start over

questions.explanation: Section 3.5 states that if a qualification fails to meet the acceptance criteria, the cause of the failure should first be investigated and addressed before the activity is repeated. Relaxing the criteria or ignoring the failure does not meet the document's requirements; deviations from the protocol must be handled under the established quality procedures.

questions.question: At close-out, a team compiles many "observations." According to section 3.6.3, what makes something a true lesson learned rather than merely an observation?

options.A: It is raised verbally by senior staff at a meeting and recorded in the minutes
options.B: The observations are sorted by time of occurrence and handed to the receiving unit for safekeeping
options.C: It includes the observation, prioritization, and an action and monitoring plan; observations without action may lead to recurrence of the event
options.D: The same event has occurred in two or more projects, in which case it is automatically regarded as a lesson learned

questions.explanation: The document states that lessons learned can include the observation, prioritization, and an action and monitoring plan; the key is the effectiveness and sustainability of the action. Observations without action may allow the event to recur, and depending on the impact a CAPA can be created and tracked in the QMS.

questions.question: The receiving unit is to implement a compendial method (for example, pH or osmolality). According to Table 4.1, which transfer approach is most suitable?

options.A: Qualitative method transfer study, which usually needs no comparison of data and is carried out as training
options.B: Quantitative method transfer study, which usually requires comparison of data and applies to assay and impurities
options.C: Method co-validation, in which the receiving unit and the development laboratory take part in validation together and assess reproducibility between sites
options.D: Method verification, performed at least once at the receiving unit with all appropriate sample types, with performance verified against specifications or historical trends

questions.explanation: Table 4.1 recommends method verification for compendial methods (such as pH and osmolality). Qualitative transfer applies to appearance, NIR identification, and the like; quantitative transfer applies to assay, bioassay, and impurities; and co-validation is where the receiving unit and the development laboratory validate together.

questions.question: What does the Analytical Target Profile (ATP) mentioned in Chapter 4 mainly define?

options.A: The instrument model, software version, and supplier list of consumables that the analytical method must use
options.B: The objective of the test, including the maximum measurement uncertainty allowed for the reportable result
options.C: The training hours and sign-off level that the receiving unit's analysts must complete
options.D: The temperature and transit time limits for shipping samples from the sending unit to the receiving unit

questions.explanation: The ATP is similar in concept to the QTPP of ICH Q8(R2); it defines the purpose of the test and the maximum measurement uncertainty allowed for the reportable result, and is generally present for methods developed under QbD principles. Instruments, training, and transport belong to other items.

questions.question: In an analytical method transfer plan, statistical tests are used to show that the results of two units are comparable. What equivalency criterion does the guide give as an example?

options.A: The two-sided 90% confidence interval (or two one-sided 95% limits) for the difference between the units must fall entirely within pre-established limits
options.B: The two-sided 95% confidence interval for the difference between the units must include zero, and the means of the two units must be identical to pass
options.C: One end of the two-sided 99% confidence interval for the difference between the units need only fall within pre-established limits
options.D: As long as the relative standard deviation of each unit is below 5%, there is no need to compare the difference between the units

questions.explanation: Section 4.2.5 explains that the equivalency criterion requires the two-sided 90% CI (or two one-sided 95% limits) for the difference between the two units to fall entirely within pre-established limits. The example in Table 4.5 also uses the 90% CI to judge whether equivalency is Met.

questions.question: The receiving unit may not get it right the first time, or the method may be more complex than its experience. Which activity should be used to identify in detail the differences in how the method is operated at the two units?

options.A: Technical risk assessment, focusing on high-level analytical issues when the method is introduced to a new environment, such as frequent system suitability failures
options.B: A test-a-batch exercise, used to assess the receiving unit's readiness and to design training and experiments
options.C: Operational risk assessment, using process mapping and Ishikawa diagrams to systematically identify sources of variation between the two units
options.D: Applying for a waiver on a scientific rationale to exempt the method transfer study and directly use the sending unit's data

questions.explanation: Section 4.2.3.2 states that when the receiving unit may not get it right the first time or the method is more complex, an operational risk assessment can be done to identify in detail the differences in how the method is operated at the two units, and it recommends process mapping and Ishikawa diagrams. A technical risk assessment deals with higher-level technical risks.

questions.question: During analytical method transfer execution, one data point deviates from expectations, and the analyst wants to exclude it from the evaluation. According to section 4.2.6, how should this be handled?

options.A: Whenever data deviate from expectations, the receiving unit may exclude them in the report and rerun, with no separate documented scientific rationale or approval record
options.B: The sending unit's supervisor may agree verbally to exclude it, with no documented rationale
options.C: Wait until all results are complete and the acceptance criteria are confirmed, then decide whether to exclude the data point
options.D: Data must not be excluded without a documented, scientifically justified reason; the protocol must specify the handling in advance

questions.explanation: Section 4.2.6 states that the protocol criteria should include the statistical methods and provisions for handling conditions that deviate from expectations and nonconforming data; data must not be excluded from further consideration without a documented, scientifically justified reason.

questions.question: In the initial feasibility assessment for a drug substance, what is the main purpose of the mass balance?

options.A: To show the correct sequence of process steps and identify all process streams, including waste and by-products
options.B: To define plant capacity and highlight where equipment changes may be needed, for example in a macromolecule process with low yield and high concentration
options.C: To establish key supply chain, analytical complexity, and safety constraints as the basis for raw material risk
options.D: To confirm the pharmacopoeial requirements of the target market and explain the reasons for differences from existing pharmacopoeias

questions.explanation: Section 5.2.1 explains that the mass balance defines plant capacity and points out where equipment changes may be needed (for example, for macromolecules where the harvest titer is low and the final concentration is high), and is also used to select a suitable receiving unit; for small molecules it provides the composition of process streams. Showing the sequence of steps and identifying all process streams is the BFD, establishing key supply chain and safety constraints is the raw material assessment, and confirming pharmacopoeial requirements is the product specification.

questions.question: Comparing the Block Flow Diagram (BFD) and the Process Flow Diagram (PFD), which of the following is consistent with section 5.2.2.1?

options.A: A PFD is usually easier to draw than a BFD, so it is best for quickly comparing process options and confirming all process streams and by-products
options.B: A BFD is mainly used to present detailed data such as processing times and in-process tests, whereas a PFD shows only the sequence of steps
options.C: A BFD is a Lean tool that is easier to produce and confirms the sequence of steps and identifies all process streams, including waste and by-products
options.D: Only one of the BFD and the PFD can be chosen, and neither can be used to support updates of regulatory filings

questions.explanation: The BFD is a Lean tool that ensures the process steps and sequence are understood and all process streams are identified; because it is easier to produce, it allows quick comparison of process options. The PFD is what visualizes key data such as processing times and in-process tests, and PFDs from earlier sites or scales are helpful for regulatory filing updates.

questions.question: In a macromolecule purification process, chromatography steps control quality through buffer pH and conductivity; the two sites use instruments of different brands, which may produce small measurement differences. What risk mitigation does the guide recommend?

options.A: Exchange buffer samples between the two sites to compare measurements; if necessary apply an offset in the receiving unit's documents, and document the experiment
options.B: Simply relax the receiving unit's pH specification, with no separate experiment and no explanation in the documents, treating it as a routine specification adjustment signed off by the receiving unit alone
options.C: Require the sending unit to switch to the receiving unit's instruments and revalidate its entire approved process
options.D: Regard the instrument difference as normal, and decide whether to address it only if results exceed specification after PPQ

questions.explanation: The risk mitigation example in section 5.2.3 is to send buffer samples between sites for comparison, take the differences into account, and apply an offset in the receiving unit's documents if needed. Such an experiment must be documented to provide traceability and rationale, because it might otherwise look like a specification change during the transfer.

questions.question: According to section 5.2.4, what is the definition of an engineering run?

options.A: A complete process rehearsal at laboratory scale, used to train staff and verify buffer formulation, whose batch data can be used for release
options.B: A batch run on a CMO's pilot equipment, intended to produce clinical drug and to be released
options.C: The first PPQ batch intended for release, whose data directly support the regulatory filing
options.D: A full-scale trial run using the intended procedures on the same equipment that will be used for GMP production, not intended for release or use

questions.explanation: The document defines an engineering run as a full-scale trial run, using the intended procedures, on the same equipment that will be used for GMP manufacture, with no intention to release the product for use. The early full-scale runs can also be GMP runs intended for release, depending on the risk and the mitigation strategy.

questions.topic: Completion point of a clinical transfer
questions.question: A project manager must define the "completion" boundary for the transfer of a clinical-stage drug substance. According to section 5.2.5.1, when can it generally be regarded as complete?

options.A: After three consecutive PPQ batches are completed and marketing authorization approval is obtained, and management signs off the transfer report
options.B: After the clinical batch supply has been manufactured and the investigational new drug (IND) filing has been submitted
options.C: After the first-year CPV report is completed and approved by management
options.D: After review of the engineering batch data is complete and the receiving unit has signed for the technology transfer package

questions.explanation: Section 5.2.5.1 states that the transfer of a clinical product may be regarded as complete once the clinical batch supply has been manufactured and the IND has been filed; for a commercial-to-commercial transfer, it is after successful commercial-scale validation at the receiving unit and completion of the required regulatory filings. The boundary should be agreed with management in a formal way such as the charter.

questions.topic: Timing of drug product transfer to commercial site
questions.question: According to section 6.1, at what point does transfer of a drug product to the intended commercial manufacturing site traditionally occur?

options.A: Between Phase 1 and Phase 2, so that the first toxicology batch is obtained at the commercial site and commercial production can begin immediately
options.B: After Phase 3 ends and before the marketing application is filed, at which point the commercial process is first established
options.C: Between Phase 2 and Phase 3, so that Phase 3 and pivotal stability batches are manufactured in the commercial facility
options.D: After marketing authorization is obtained, when the commercial site's process fit is assessed for the first time

questions.explanation: Section 6.1 states that this activity traditionally occurs between Phase 2 and Phase 3, so that Phase 3 and pivotal stability supply are manufactured in the commercial facility. This also supports lifecycle validation and builds manufacturing experience at the commercial facility.

questions.question: In the initial feasibility assessment for a drug product transfer, what additional consideration applies to aseptic processes?

options.A: The receiving facility's ability to maintain aseptic areas, assuming the facility already has appropriate controls such as HEPA filtration, air classification, and gowning procedures
options.B: Only the receiving unit's capacity needs to be confirmed; aseptic control is assessed after PPQ and can be arranged later by the receiving unit's quality department on its own
options.C: Whether the receiving facility uses aseptic filling equipment of the same brand as the sending unit, in which case other controls can be skipped
options.D: Whether the sending unit's personnel can perform the aseptic operations throughout at the receiving unit, to reduce contamination risk

questions.explanation: Section 6.2.1 states that for aseptic processes the facility's ability to maintain aseptic areas should be additionally considered, assuming the receiving facility already has appropriate controls (such as HEPA filtration, air classification, and gowning procedures). The feasibility assessment must be performed by a cross-functional team covering process, analytical, supply chain, operations, HSE, and quality.

questions.question: When planning the number of PPQ lots, which recommendation does section 7.6 give?

options.A: Ten lots are required in every regulatory region worldwide, cannot be adjusted for the amount of product knowledge, and need not be discussed with the authority
options.B: As long as a single batch result meets specification, the other batches can be replaced by the sending unit's historical data
options.C: Three non-consecutive batches are the basis, and engineering batches may be interspersed between them as needed
options.D: Many regions use at least three consecutive successful batches, but the number can be adjusted up or down with knowledge, and direct consultation with the authority on the transfer strategy is recommended

questions.explanation: Section 7.6 states that many regulatory regions use at least three consecutive successful batches, but other authorities may accept more or fewer depending on product knowledge. The number of batches must also account for the batches needed for analytical comparability and stability, and direct consultation with the authority is recommended.

questions.topic: Intrinsic vs extrinsic deviation in PPQ
questions.question: A deviation occurs in the second PPQ batch and causes product failure; the investigation confirms the root cause lies in the process itself (intrinsic). According to section 7.8, what is the effect on the consecutive PPQ batches?

options.A: Consecutiveness is not affected; the third batch can proceed directly, with the deviation simply noted in the report
options.B: The consecutiveness of the batches is broken, and the run will most likely need to be repeated
options.C: Only the acceptance criteria in the PPQ protocol need to be revised; batches do not need to be repeated
options.D: The receiving unit decides on its own whether to repeat, with no formal investigation or CAPA needed

questions.explanation: Section 7.8 explains that consecutive batches are generally needed to show the process is in control; a deviation related to the process itself (intrinsic) that causes product failure will most likely require a repeat because consecutiveness has been broken. If the root cause lies outside the process (extrinsic), consecutiveness is usually not broken. Every deviation still requires formal investigation and corrective action.

questions.question: Comparing the analytical comparability needed for early clinical-stage and commercial-stage products, which statement is correct according to section 7.5?

options.A: Early and commercial stages have identical requirements; the number of batches and the scope of testing do not change across the lifecycle, and prior data need not be considered
options.B: The early stage needs more batches because it has the most prior nonclinical and clinical data
options.C: As the product matures, expectations and requirements rise; fewer batches can be used early, while the commercial stage usually needs more batches to show consistency
options.D: The commercial stage can rely only on release testing, with no characterization and no need to set evaluation criteria in advance

questions.explanation: Section 7.5 explains that early-stage products have limited prior data, so comparability testing is usually less extensive than for late-stage or approved products. The number of batches needed is driven mainly by lifecycle stage; fewer can be justified early, and the commercial stage may need more. Evaluation criteria should be established prospectively.

questions.question: In the transfer information checklist in Appendix 1, which of the following falls under the "Facility and Equipment" category?

options.A: P&IDs (piping and instrumentation diagrams)
options.B: Process Hazard Risk Analysis
options.C: Master Batch Record(s)
options.D: Quality Agreements

questions.explanation: The Facility and Equipment category of the checklist includes P&IDs, URS/Design Specifications, Utilities Requirements, Control System(s), and so on. Process Hazard Risk Analysis belongs to HSE, the Master Batch Record belongs to Process, and Quality Agreements belong to Quality/Regulatory.

questions.question: When the case chapter discusses CMO selection, it recommends that the RFP contain sufficient process detail. What is the reason, and what process is recommended?

options.A: So the CMO can simply quote directly, with no need to compare different responses; one round of proposals is enough to finish contract negotiation and sign the quality agreement
options.B: So the CMO can design the process independently, and the client need not provide any more development reports or batch records
options.C: To shorten the CMO's review time, so the RFP should be limited to the product name and target delivery date
options.D: So that the responses can be compared and the CMO can assess whether it can deliver; one to two rounds of proposal refinement are usually needed to compare accurately

questions.explanation: Section 9.3.1 states that sufficient process detail makes the proposals received comparable and lets the CMO assess whether it can execute the process and meet the timeline; there are usually at least one to two rounds of proposal refinement, which helps accurate comparison and contract negotiation. The RFP should also include analytical methods, specifications, the BOM, and target dates.

questions.question: A small or mid-sized biotech company lacks development history and process knowledge and plans to transfer its process to a CMO. According to section 9.2, what is one key to success?

options.A: After the CMO completes the first GMP batch, the CMO performs the gap assessment, which is delivered to the client only at close-out
options.B: Perform a gap assessment before the transfer and share it with the CMO at initiation to achieve alignment and ensure transparency
options.C: Conceal knowledge gaps to preserve bargaining power, and provide information gradually only after the contract is signed
options.D: Rely entirely on the CMO's procedures, with the client's production team taking part only after the GMP batch is completed

questions.explanation: Section 9.2 states that performing a gap assessment before starting the transfer and sharing it with the CMO at initiation, to achieve alignment and ensure transparency, is critical to success. The manufacturing team should also be involved early in the transfer and development phases.

questions.question: In Biologics Case Study 3, the receiving unit found at laboratory-scale evaluation that the pH of the Protein A eluate was clearly lower than expected. Which of the following is closest to the root cause?

options.A: The receiving unit used a fast flow resin rather than a high performance resin, causing a difference in loading capacity
options.B: The two sites calibrate their pH meters differently, causing a fixed measurement bias
options.C: Only the buffer name was provided at transfer, without preparation details; the two units differed in salt form and in the acid used for titration
options.D: The elution flow rate was set incorrectly at scale-up, so the product stayed too long at pH 3.2

questions.explanation: Case 3 used an Ishikawa diagram to find that only the buffer name, not the preparation details, was shared at transfer. The sending unit used the trihydrate salt and titrated with hydrochloric acid, while the receiving unit used the anhydrous salt and titrated with acetic acid, giving a much higher buffering capacity. Loading capacity differences between fast flow and high performance resins were the resin issue in Case 5.

questions.question: In Case 2, the new cell line was still in development, and the MCB could not be obtained because of testing delays and inconsistent receipt requirements across the CMO sites. How did the team handle this?

options.A: They set acceptance criteria: the RCB for development use and the MCB for GMP use; small-scale work started with the RCB, switching over once the MCB became available
options.B: They suspended all work until the MCB was obtained and met the receipt requirements of all CMO sites, and only then started any small-scale experiments and media testing
options.C: They manufactured GMP batches directly from the RCB and released them, then confirmed later using the MCB
options.D: They replaced it with another existing cell line and explained in the transfer documents that only the original CMO's records needed to be reused

questions.explanation: Case 2 established acceptance criteria of RCB for development and MCB for GMP, so that small-scale work could start with the RCB and switch to the MCB once available, avoiding project waiting. Manufacturing GMP batches from the RCB, or halting work to wait for materials, were not approaches described in the document.

questions.topic: Main challenge in global API transfers
questions.question: Section 10.2 states that for API transfers within a global supply chain, which differences between the sending and receiving units must be identified early?

options.A: Only differences in equipment brand and model; other systems are managed uniformly by the two headquarters
options.B: Only differences in raw material suppliers and packaging specifications; the quality system does not vary by site
options.C: Only differences in headcount and shift patterns, which have nothing to do with regulatory or compliance standards
options.D: Differences in QMS, risk tolerance, and operational and compliance standards, so they can be incorporated into the overall transfer plan

questions.explanation: Section 10.2 states that the transfer must take into account the differences between the sending and receiving units in QMS, risk tolerance, and operational and compliance standards, and that these must be identified early in the transfer so they can be addressed in the overall transfer plan.

questions.topic: Small Molecule Case Study #1 CPP interpretation
questions.question: In Small Molecule Case 1, the documentation designated the flowrate of a reactant as a critical parameter (0.5-1.0 L/min), but the batch record actually measured only the total addition time. What does this example mainly illustrate?

options.A: The receiving unit should directly replace flowrate with total time as the critical parameter, and update the entire process validation, batch record, and critical parameter list accordingly
options.B: The written explanation of criticality and the actual operating practice may not be consistent, so face-to-face communication and talking with the people on the floor are needed to understand actual practice
options.C: The flowrate range is too wide and should be redefined by the sending unit before any transfer work can proceed
options.D: The batch record being in a foreign language is the only problem; once translated there will be no other gaps in understanding

questions.explanation: Case 1 showed that the sending unit's common way of managing flowrate (measuring total time) differed slightly from the documented criticality explanation, and with a language barrier it was hard for the receiving unit to understand actual practice. The solution was face-to-face meetings, with technicians who had hands-on operating experience taking part.

questions.topic: Small Molecule Case Study #2 method counts
questions.question: In Small Molecule Case 2, after the two sites' QMS were harmonized, how many analytical method activities did the overall technology transfer plan finally include?

options.A: 21 method verification/qualification and 80 full method validation
options.B: 8 method verification/qualification and 80 full method validation
options.C: 80 method verification/qualification and 8 full method validation
options.D: 88 full method validation, with no verification or qualification

questions.explanation: The overall plan in Case 2 included 80 method verification/qualification activities and 8 full validations. The hybrid approach also changed 21 methods from validation to verification/qualification, saving one analyst more than a year of time.

questions.topic: Small Molecule Case Study #3 scale-up lesson
questions.question: In Small Molecule Case 3, after scale-up of more than 10-fold and start-up at commercial scale, new critical parameters were found that had not been seen at laboratory stage. According to the case's conclusion, how should the project plan respond?

options.A: Include a commercial-scale demonstration batch in the project plan, and include extended hold times in laboratory development
options.B: Simply add more batches in the laboratory, because a few more laboratory reproducibility batches would cover all scale-up risks and safety concerns
options.C: Avoid any safety assessment before commercial scale, so as not to delay equipment design and validation timelines
options.D: Go directly to PPQ after pilot scale, because parameters such as mixing can be fully simulated in the laboratory

questions.explanation: The conclusion of Case 3 is that parameters such as mixing are difficult to simulate in a development laboratory or even at pilot scale, so a commercial-scale demonstration batch should be included in the plan; laboratory development should also include extended hold times to simulate commercial manufacturing. Safety considerations and reaction kinetic modeling are also important. In the case, new critical parameters appeared at commercial start-up even though 3 laboratory reproducibility batches had been run.

questions.question: The extraction step in Case 3 formed an emulsion. Which of the following is the cause and the remedy?

options.A: Insufficient mixing caused locally high acid concentration; it was eliminated by raising the agitation speed
options.B: Raw material left standing too long in the drum precipitated solids; a vacuum dip tube was used to draw off the clear solution
options.C: The cooling system could not hold -5°C; an orifice plate was used to control the flow rate of the limiting reagent
options.D: It resulted from overmixing; a pressure transfer replaced the centrifugal pump, and mixing in the extraction vessel was reduced by 65%

questions.explanation: In Table 10.6, the emulsion was caused by overmixing during extraction, and the fix was to replace the centrifugal pump with a pressure transfer and reduce mixing by 65%. "Insufficient mixing, raise the agitation speed" belongs to a different problem (too little mixing during acid neutralization produced unknown impurities, so mixing had to be increased); "switch to a vacuum dip tube" belongs to the raw material drum sedimentation problem.

questions.question: The receiving unit must procure or operate equipment that is "similar but not identical" to the sending unit's in order to complete the process. According to section 11.1, where is the focus in this case?

options.A: The focus is on equipment use and behavior, because the equipment is identical to the sending unit's
options.B: The focus is on the equipment's recommended configuration and setup details, because each side owns the same equipment
options.C: The focus is on the product and process outcomes; the way the outcome is achieved can be different
options.D: The focus is on equipment appearance and nameplate data; as long as the models are close, no other assessment is needed

questions.explanation: Section 11.1 lists three scenarios. When equipment is like-for-like, the focus is knowledge of use and behavior; when each side has the same or similar equipment, operating experience and recommended configuration and setup details are needed; when it is similar but not identical, the product and process outcomes matter most, and the way of achieving them may differ.

questions.question: Example #1: three sites bought the same powder inhaler filling equipment, and a part wore over time, increasing fill weight variability; one site found the root cause, while the others blamed something else. What is the lesson learned in Table 11.7?

options.A: Include feedback loops in the transfer plan so that new knowledge gained by the receiving unit benefits the whole organization
options.B: When planning the transfer, ask the receiving unit for its existing engineering knowledge on equipment selection
options.C: In addition to reviewing validation activities, also review the engineering work that supports them
options.D: Review the configuration information in the control system to make sure the latest content is captured

questions.explanation: The lesson in Table 11.7 for Example #1 is to include feedback loops. Asking the receiving unit for its existing engineering knowledge corresponds to Example #2 (instrument drift), reviewing the supporting engineering work beyond validation activities corresponds to Example #4 (maintenance frequency and priority), and reviewing control system configuration information corresponds to Example #6 (automation configuration).

questions.question: A mAb process was transferred from the US to Europe, and because existing equipment was used, no commissioning was planned. Problems occurred in the UF/DF concentration stage of the first large-scale run. What did the investigation find?

options.A: The wrong UF membrane model was selected, giving an insufficient concentration factor; replacing the membrane fixes it, with no need to repeat the batch or investigate other systems
options.B: The automation recipe had not been configured correctly; the batch was impacted and was repeated under a CAPA, and Quality and Validation felt the investigation should be expanded to the configuration of other systems
options.C: A temperature instrument drifted over time and caused product content to deviate; both sites must replace the instrument and redo qualification and calibration
options.D: A filling machine part wore and increased weight variability, so a trigger point for periodic maintenance needs to be established

questions.explanation: The root cause in Example #6 was an incorrectly configured automation recipe; commissioning was not done because no new equipment was started up. The batch was therefore impacted and had to be repeated. Engineering considered the misconfigured item non-critical, but Quality and Validation felt the investigation should be expanded to whether the configuration of other systems was appropriate. The lesson is to review control system configuration information. Instrument drift and filling machine part wear are Example #2 and Example #1 respectively.

questions.question: Two sites claim to use equipment of the same brand and model and the same material specifications. According to the engineering equivalence assessment in section 11.3.1, how should this be viewed?

options.A: As long as brand, model, and materials are the same, the comparison can be skipped because performance will necessarily be consistent
options.B: Only equipment purchase dates and warranty terms need to be compared, because performance differences are mainly caused by equipment age
options.C: Only the two sites' SOP versions need to be compared; differences in equipment and utility systems are outside the assessment scope, so design specifications need not be compared separately
options.D: Even when systems look the same, performance may still differ; design and specifications, performance data under similar inputs and operating conditions, and engineering data should be compared

questions.explanation: Section 11.3.1 states that even when the process and equipment are considered identical (same brand, model, starting materials, and specifications), the systems may still perform differently. An equivalence assessment compares the design and specifications of the equipment and utilities, performance data under similar inputs and operating conditions, and engineering data.

questions.question: Engineering SMEs from both sides meet (preferably face to face) after receiving the project scope and process description. What does section 11.3.1 recommend about the responsibilities matrix?

options.A: The receiving unit writes it after project close-out, because actual roles will become clear only once operations begin
options.B: The sending unit prepares it, taking into account the receiving unit's capability and maturity for this transfer project
options.C: The equipment supplier drafts it because it knows the equipment best, and the SMEs of both sides only sign off
options.D: The project manager drafts it alone, and the engineering SMEs need not take part in discussing roles and skills

questions.explanation: The document recommends that the meeting outcome include a list of required deliverables and a responsibilities matrix; the sending unit should prepare the matrix, considering the receiving unit's capability and maturity. The content covers engineering SME roles, a skills matrix, and supplier and vendor roles.

questions.question: According to the Glossary, which is the definition of a Critical Process Parameter (CPP)?

options.A: A process parameter whose variability has an impact on a CQA and therefore should be monitored or controlled to ensure the process produces the desired quality
options.B: A physical, chemical, biological, or microbiological property or characteristic that should be within an appropriate limit, range, or distribution to ensure the desired product quality
options.C: A prospective summary of the quality characteristics of a drug product that ideally will be achieved to ensure the desired quality, taking into account safety and efficacy
options.D: A planned set of controls, derived from current product and process understanding, that ensures process performance and product quality

questions.explanation: A CPP is a process parameter whose variability has an impact on a CQA and therefore should be monitored or controlled. The definition of a property that should be within an appropriate limit is the CQA, the prospective summary of quality characteristics of a drug product is the QTPP, and the planned set of controls derived from current product and process understanding is the control strategy.

questions.question: The Glossary includes the FDA and EMA definitions of process validation. Which comparison is correct?

options.A: They are identical, and both are three-stage lifecycle definitions covering process design through commercial production
options.B: The FDA definition refers to a single stage only, while the EMA definition covers the full lifecycle from process design to commercial production; the scope is exactly the opposite
options.C: The FDA definition is a lifecycle definition covering three stages; the EMA definition is a single-stage definition, equivalent to Stage 2.2 (PPQ) of the FDA guidance
options.D: Both apply only to the commercial production stage and do not cover process design and development activities

questions.explanation: The FDA definition is the collection and evaluation of data from process design through commercial production to establish scientific evidence, covering three stages. The EMA definition is documented evidence that the process, operated within established parameters, can perform effectively and reproducibly to produce a medicinal product meeting its predetermined specifications; it refers to a single stage, equivalent to Stage 2.2 of the FDA guidance.

questions.question: The FMEA example table in Appendix 5 contains SEV, OCC, DET, and RPN columns. From which items is the RPN (Risk Priority Number) derived?

options.A: Severity, cost, and delivery time, used to prioritize allocation of the project budget
options.B: Occurrence, preventability, and responsible unit, used to decide who owns corrective actions and when the related preventive actions are completed
options.C: Severity, detectability, and batch size, used to decide the sampling quantity for each batch
options.D: Severity (impact), occurrence (probability), and detection, used to determine the risk level and whether mitigation is needed

questions.explanation: Section 5.2.3 states that considering severity, occurrence, and detection yields the RPN, which is the basis for determining the risk level and whether mitigation is needed. The Appendix 5 example is an FMEA of tableting and IPC controls for a non-sterile drug product, with columns SEV, OCC, DET, and RPN.

questions.question: The sample technology transfer report in Appendix 6 divides information into Development Information and Production Information. Which of the following is Production Information?

options.A: Formulation Development Report
options.B: List of all Lots Manufactured
options.C: Excipient Compatibility Report
options.D: Justification of Specifications

questions.explanation: Production Information includes the List of all Lots Manufactured, the various batch protocols and reports, Bills of Material, the list of MBR versions, and so on. The Formulation Development Report, Excipient Compatibility Report, and Justification of Specifications are all Development Information.

questions.question: According to the Glossary, what is the relationship between the User Requirement Specification (URS) and the Functional Requirement Specification (FRS)?

options.A: The URS builds on the FRS and provides a basic description of the functions the control system is expected to perform
options.B: They are different names for the same document, with identical content and purpose
options.C: The FRS builds on the URS and describes the functions the process and control system are expected to perform; the URS describes the facility's requirements for the product, capacity, and conditions
options.D: The FRS replaces the URS once equipment qualification is complete, so the URS no longer needs to be retained or updated under change control

questions.explanation: The Glossary states that the FRS builds on the URS and provides a basic description of the functions the process and control system are expected to perform; the URS describes the facility's requirements for the product to be manufactured, the capacity needed, and the production conditions.
